en: This duty is not a new law with a name of its own. It comes from the duty to inform, from good faith and from making the consumer's defense easier, which the law already provides. It does not require opening all of the system's code or making the company's secrets public. The examination must be limited to what matters for the case, preserving the necessary confidentiality.
You may still be inside the service, with your account, seeing the item and logging in whenever you want, and still have lost the main thing. Keeping it working is not the same as keeping its value.

The platform must preserve, in substance, the role the item had in your experience. That includes what it does, the relationship it creates with other people and, when it matters to the law, what it means.

The platform may update the service, and no one demands that the item stay identical forever or that the service stand still in time. Many changes are, in fact, the natural evolution of the environment. The problem is the change that puts on you the cost of seriously worsening what you bought, without restoration that measures up.

On your side, it helps to tell plausibly what you went through, to show how it fits into the way the platform works and to gather what was within your reach. On the platform's side, it is up to it to present the records, histories, versions and technical justifications that matter for the case.

When the problem affects your access, the continuity of what you use or the equivalence of what you bought. Or when it affects your history, your position in front of other people or the weight that thing had for you.

The platform must make what was advertised match what is delivered. The promise, the advertised value and the costs that did not show must match the experience you get, even after the platform changes the rules.
Not every way of selling, persuading or running the service is abusive. What is controlled is a program recognizable in how the environment works, not someone's hidden will.

When the company uses the rights it holds over the game, the program or the content to resist any control over the way it supplies what you bought. This includes copyright, trade secrets, licenses and control over the system itself.
It helps to show whether the restriction the company invokes is really necessary to protect the work, or whether it is serving to shield the way it governs the environment.

The central request is that consumer law keep applying. In practice, this may mean a limited examination of the records that preserves secrets, and control over the equivalence of what you bought. It may also mean that the company respects the duties of adequacy, transparency and restoration. And, if the service is shut down, that the exit comes, as far as possible, with transition, preservation or transfer of what you had inside.

The intellectual property rights over the work, the art and the code remain protected. No one asks the company to give up the work. What is at issue is using that exclusivity as a general veto against consumer protection.

Almost everything you know about what you bought comes through screens, notices, icons and paths the platform designs. It is through them that you find out how much it is worth, what risk you run when buying and how to complain if something goes wrong. When your expectation and your chance to contest depend on these signals controlled by the company, you are in a fragile position. And the law takes that fragility into account.

It helps to show the path you took inside the platform up to the purchase or the problem, what was highlighted on the screen and where the information went. The records that allow reconstructing how your expectation was formed also matter. Dated screenshots, screen recordings and the purchase and confirmation screens help, because they show how the environment was set up, and not only what you remember.

This does not mean that every complicated service violates rights, nor that you are incapable in the face of the digital. The fragility that counts is the one that appears when the signals controlled by the platform steer your expectation or hinder your reaction.
Almost everything you know about what you bought comes through screens, notices, icons and paths the platform designs. It is through them that you find out how much…

First, a word of caution. None of this is a ready formula or a guarantee of results, because each case depends on what happened, on what can be proved and on how whoever decides reads the facts. What changes is the way of telling the conflict, which stops being an isolated episode and becomes the way the platform supplies what it sold.
When the company uses the rights it holds over the game, the program or the content to resist any control over the way it supplies what…
